title: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System
author: Anthea Roberts · Taylor St John

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions
st.an: The source does not evaluate whether disruption theory’s historical examples fit its causal predictions. Instead, it offers a different, qualified account of why outsiders may innovate: distance from entrenched assumptions can foster creativity, while some expertise remains beneficial. This reframes the issue around outsider cognition rather than validating Christensen’s market-entry and displacement mechanism.
qs: From this broad literature, we  draw out three characteristics that make outsiders more likely than insiders to develop  disruptive innovations.
The first characteristic is freedom from accumulated common sense in a field, which  can lead outsiders to be more open to new ideas or fresh ways of seeing things.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses how officials’ insider–outsider status shapes ISDS reform proposals, not legal AI capability, verification, selective deployment or work redesign. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to assess the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Institutional reform: Outsider ideas need insider adoption
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that outsider status can foster disruptive originality while limiting uptake. Its case studies associate outsider officials with proposals that displace existing arrangements, and it acknowledges that outsiders may lack the recognition needed for diffusion. It does not itself develop the cluster’s fuller prescription of insider–outsider coalitions.
qs: This pattern ech- oes observations about innovation in other fields: insiders are more likely to propose  innovations with the intention of sustaining and updating existing practices, whereas  outsiders are more likely to develop innovations that may disrupt or displace existing  practices.

st.t: Reform networks: Background shapes but cannot determine innovation
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: officials’ proximity to investment-arbitration practice shapes whether they pursue sustaining or disruptive reforms, while background remains only one influence among several. It also separates proposal generation from normative quality and eventual adoption, rejecting a deterministic account.
qs: Our argument  is that outsider status increases the chances that officials will develop disruptive in- novations, as one of a number of factors influencing state policy.

kp.k: Outsider backgrounds help explain disruptive investment arbitration reform
kp.d: The article examines investment treaty reform, not AI. Roberts and St John argue that officials outside investor-state arbitration are more likely to propose disruptive reforms, while insiders tend toward sustaining reforms. This is a dispositional explanation alongside economic position, policy ideology and dispute experience, not a claim that backgrounds alone determine policy or that disruptive reforms are superior.
qs: Our argument  is that outsider status increases the chances that officials will develop disruptive in- novations, as one of a number of factors influencing state policy.

In identifying  this pattern, our argument is not normative or predictive; we do not take a stand on  whether disruptive or sustaining reforms are better or worse, or which ones are likely  to be adopted by other states.

kp.k: Evidence combines sustained observation and interviews
kp.d: The authors draw on five years of para-ethnographic observation and interviews, attending every UNCITRAL Working Group III session since 2017. They report 10 full weeks of formal sessions, another 30 days of related meetings and substantive interactions with 15 delegations on average during each full week. Purposive sampling sought diversity in region and reform perspectives; their interpretation emerged iteratively through observation, interviews and innovation literature rather than a quantified causal test.
qs: Since 2017, we have attended 10 full weeks of  Working Group III formal sessions, plus a further 30 days of informal sessions, inter- sessionals and UNCITRAL Commission sessions.
We use a purposive sampling strategy,  selecting actors who represent the breadth of views at UNCITRAL.
We drew our conclusions from this iterative, dialectical  process.

kp.k: Sustaining and disruptive innovations form a spectrum
kp.d: Drawing on business scholarship, the authors distinguish improvements that preserve an existing product or practice from innovations threatening to replace it. They explicitly treat these categories as ideal types along a spectrum. Applied to ISDS, reforms range from procedural adjustments to permanent adjudicative institutions and alternatives that displace investor-state arbitration.
qs: Such sustaining and disruptive  innovations are not binary.
Instead, they represent ideal types at either end of a spec- trum, so innovations can be more or less sustaining or disruptive.

kp.k: Expertise can constrain innovation through cognitive entrenchment
kp.d: The innovation literature reviewed suggests that outsiders face fewer intellectual and social constraints from established assumptions. Expertise can improve capability while narrowing flexibility; the authors describe an inverted U-shaped relationship between knowledge and creativity. These are mechanisms drawn from other disciplines, not measured effects established by the four investment-policy cases.
qs: The more expertise and experience people gain within a field, the more entrenched  they often become in a particular worldview, making it harder to innovate in more  creative or far-reaching ways.
Outsiders bring fresh eyes to an existing system, enabling them  to question established truths and accepted wisdom.

kp.k: Boundary crossing and weaker vested interests enable disruption
kp.d: The authors identify two further mechanisms: outsiders can translate insights between fields, and they are less likely to possess financial or reputational interests in preserving existing arrangements. Insiders' specialized knowledge and dense networks instead support developing and spreading sustaining innovations. Outsiders' weaker recognition within a field can impede uptake even while incumbents underestimate their proposals.
qs: Individuals who cross between fields are likely to be able to trans- late insights from one field into another or to be more flexible in their thinking and  better able to combine insights in novel ways.
A third trait of outsiders is that they are unlikely to have vested financial and repu- tational interests that would lead them to favour sustaining innovations over disrup- tive ones.

Although freedom from the accumulated common sense within a field can foster in- novation, outsiders may lack the recognition necessary for their innovative proposals  to be taken seriously within a field, at least initially.

kp.k: EU competence transfer empowered outsiders advocating permanent courts
kp.d: After the Treaty of Lisbon transferred investment-policy competence in 2009, routine allocation placed ISDS policy in DG Trade's legal unit rather than its litigation service. The initial team grew from one member in 2010 to two in 2011 and three in 2012, without backgrounds in arbitral practice. The authors connect its trade-law experience and distance from arbitration to a multilateral investment court proposal with an appellate mechanism, retaining substantive treaty obligations and investors' ability to bring international claims.
qs: Although not necessarily intended, the effect of this routine allocation following a  shift in competence was to put outsiders at the helm of Europe’s ISDS policy.

None of the team members  had a background in arbitral practice: the team’s lead had a background in trade,  another came from tax and corporate law and a third had an academic and gov- ernment background in investment treaties but not in arbitration.

kp.k: Political pressure opened space for EU institutional change
kp.d: The authors distinguish the political opportunity for reform from the officials' influence on its design. Vattenfall and transatlantic negotiations helped mobilize opposition; the 2014 consultation received overwhelmingly negative responses, 97 per cent from civil society groups. Practitioner engagement was initially limited: only seven of nearly 150,000 submissions came from law firms. The authors interpret this as an instance of insiders initially underestimating disruptive outsiders, not evidence that the proposed court had succeeded.
qs: Only seven of the nearly 150,000 submissions were from law firms.

The reallocation of respon- sibility for ISDS with the Treaty of Lisbon enabled this group of outsiders to assume  responsibility for this policy area, while the pressure from civil society created the  crisis or window of opportunity necessary for innovation.

kp.k: US insiders innovate through iterative treaty management
kp.d: US officials' arbitration experience, private-practice connections and relatively integrated litigation and negotiation functions support sustaining reform. At the January 2020 session, at least 17 current or former US officials were present, including 14 delegates; five delegates were in private practice. The US approach uses treaty updates, non-disputing-party submissions and joint interpretations to respond to adjudication. The authors also emphasize a distinct government culture attentive to wider policy interests, rather than equating government lawyers with private counsel.
qs: This is the essence of how the USA innovates in the investment treaty system: it  negotiates with insights from litigation, and it litigates with insights from negoti- ations.

Unlike many governments  that separate negotiators and litigators into different units or even different ministries,  US practice in cases and treaties is managed in a relatively unified way and reviewed  through an interagency process, and some US officials even work on both negotiations  and disputes.

kp.k: US representatives favor existing tools over structural replacement
kp.d: The article reports the US position that existing interpretive tools should be used more systematically before introducing permanent institutions. US representatives describe these reforms as real change, despite their gradual development, and warn that standing bodies could introduce uncertain costs or consequences. These assertions concern the US policy rationale, not independently established comparative effectiveness of arbitration and courts.
qs: To the USA, the necessary tools exist, but they just have not been used  enough by other states, many of  which have less experience in ISDS.
The US insider officials see little benefit in disrupting the status  quo, preferring sustaining innovations in order to improve upon, while stabilizing, the  existing system.

kp.k: Brazil reframes investment governance around facilitation and prevention
kp.d: Brazil never ratified its 1990s investment treaties and had never been party to an ISDS dispute. Officials with trade and international economic-law experience developed the ACFI model, emphasizing investment facilitation, dispute prevention and state-to-state settlement rather than ISDS. It excludes fair and equitable treatment and incorporates an ombudsman, following South Korea's innovation. Brazil had signed 16 agreements by late 2021, including with India; its officials' suggestion that this emboldened other actors is presented as their interpretation.
qs: Thus, Brazil has never been a party to an ISDS dispute.

The model excludes controversial substantive standards, such as fair and equitable  treatment, and incorporates new features, such as an ombudsman to help deal with  investors’ concerns and grievances before they escalate into formal claims, replicating  South Korea’s innovation.
Brazil had signed 16 agreements by late  2021, including with large states like India.

kp.k: Alternative networks shape where outsiders pursue reform
kp.d: Brazil's officials participate constructively at UNCITRAL and seek room for state-to-state mechanisms, but direct their principal investment-policy efforts elsewhere. Their experience and networks support work on investment facilitation among WTO members. The authors contrast international traction for these initiatives with their marginalization in a forum focused on ISDS reform.
qs: Although Brazil participates at UNCITRAL, its principal energies in investment policy are directed elsewhere - in ways that leverage the broader networks and ex- periences of its officials.
Brazil’s innovations in investment policy-making are gaining ground inter- nationally, but these innovations have been sidelined at UNCITRAL where the focus is  on ISDS reform.

kp.k: Bahrain's arbitral insiders advocate institution-led incremental reform
kp.d: Bahrain's ambition to become an arbitration hub aligns with representation by Bahrain Chamber for Dispute Resolution specialists rather than government officials. Its proposals include institution-developed binding conduct codes, broader arbitrator pools, joint interpretive committees and annulment reforms. Representatives acknowledge their professional perspective but maintain that incrementalism matches government objectives. Their warnings that a permanent court might deter investment or increase required returns are prospective concerns, not observed outcomes.
qs: Although many states are vying to be arbitral hubs, Bahrain is the only such state  with representatives from an arbitration institution speaking for it at UNCITRAL  rather than government officials.
We think about it all the time because we are arbitration specialists.
In one such  submission, Bahrain proposed five improvements to the existing system, including  binding codes of conduct to be developed by arbitration institutions and a wider pool  of arbitrators.

kp.k: Bahrain frames geographic expansion as reform without replacement
kp.d: The authors characterize Bahrain's innovation as extending established arbitration practices to new geographic centers. Its representatives invoke developing-country interests and challenge EU leadership, portraying structural reform as recolonization just as developing countries gain experience and representation. The authors explicitly distinguish this framing from academic uses of neocolonial continuity, which commonly criticize structural reform for not going far enough.
qs: Bahrain innovates in the investment  treaty system by transplanting old practices to new geographies
In Bahrain’s view, what was wrong with arbitration was not systemic or design-related  per se; it was the under-representation of investors and arbitrators from outside the  global North.

Scholars emphasizing neo-colonial continuities often believe that structural reform efforts do not go far  enough; we are not aware of any other voices that believe reform equates with recolonization.

kp.k: Policy and personnel interact through endogenous feedback loops
kp.d: The authors caution that prior state policies influence recruitment and experience, which then shape subsequent policy. They propose research comparing bureaucratic allocations, institutional checks and shifts in responsibility to distinguish individual influence from state preferences. They also hypothesize that insider experience and potential private-sector careers could sustain support for ISDS even after costly claims; this is a research avenue, not a demonstrated general effect.
qs: A state’s general ISDS policy and officials’ backgrounds are endogenous - that is,  there are feedback loops connecting earlier policy decisions to later personnel deci- sions, which in turn shape subsequent policy decisions and so on.
Our case studies suggest that moments in which policy- making responsibility is shifted are a prime opportunity for change and for outsiders  to have influence

kp.k: Generating innovation differs from securing its diffusion
kp.d: The authors limit their central argument to proposing reforms. Their observations suggest that a represented state's weight matters more to reception than an official's insider status, while consistent attendance and substantive contributions over several years can increase respect for proposals. Whether disruptive reforms diffuse remains unresolved and may depend on state power and sustained engagement rather than the traits that initially generated them.
qs: Fourth, our argument about outsiders is limited to proposing reforms
We have observed that the weight of the state an official represents seems to be more important to the reception of the reform proposal than  the outsider or insider status of the official.

Whether those innovations get picked up by others and diffused within the system  more broadly remains to be seen and may depend on a different set of factors, such as  the relative size and power of the state and its commitment to playing a significant role  in the negotiating process over an extended period of time.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This is a cross-domain source about investment treaty reform, not AI. Roberts and St John argue that officials outside investment arbitration are more likely to develop disruptive reforms, whereas arbitral insiders tend to propose reforms that sustain the existing system.
pts.d: The authors identify officials’ backgrounds, networks and interests, together with the allocation of policy responsibility among ministries, as influences on reform proposals. Their EU and Brazil cases illustrate outsider-led alternatives: a permanent investment court for the EU, and investment facilitation, dispute prevention and state-to-state dispute settlement for Brazil. Their USA and Bahrain cases illustrate insider-led reform within arbitration: treaty interpretation and iterative treaty updating for the USA, and institution-led improvements for Bahrain. The authors distinguish originating reforms from securing their adoption; outsider characteristics may aid originality without aiding diffusion. Separately, an interviewed Bahrain delegate predicts that replacing ISDS with a court could deter investment or cause investors to demand contractual arbitration or higher returns. That is the delegate’s concern, not an established effect or the authors’ prediction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their account with five years of participant observation, interviews, negotiating records and four qualitative case studies, interpreted through interdisciplinary innovation literature.
pts.d: They report observing every UNCITRAL Working Group III session since 2017, attending 10 full weeks of formal sessions and another 30 days of related meetings, and interacting substantively with approximately 15 delegations per full week. They use purposive sampling across regions and reform perspectives, informal exchanges, loosely structured interviews, session recordings and documentary materials. Officials’ accounts connect professional backgrounds to reform choices; delegation composition and public interventions illustrate insider networks and policy positions. This is an interpretive account of a dispositional association, not a quantified causal estimate. The Bahrain delegate’s investment-risk predictions rest on professional judgment; the article does not supply measured effects of the proposed court.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The central claim concerns the origins of reform proposals observed over the five-year research period beginning in 2017, with earlier policy developments used to explain those origins; it is not a forecast of which reforms will prevail.
pts.d: The EU account traces responsibility transfers in 2009–2010 and subsequent political pressure; Brazil’s account traces policy development from the early 2010s. The authors describe insider/outsider status as one influence among economic position, policy ideology, arbitral-hub ambitions and experience of disputes. They recognize feedback loops between policy and personnel, rather than treating officials’ backgrounds as independent causes. They suggest that reallocating policy responsibility creates opportunities for outsiders, while a small number of responsible officials and limited institutional checks may increase individual influence. Their diffusion discussion remains conditional: state weight, sustained participation and officials’ credibility may matter more for adoption than outsider status. No adoption deadline is given.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed changes affect governments, foreign investors, arbitration professionals and institutions, and constituencies concerned with regulatory autonomy and dispute-system legitimacy.
pts.d: For governments, the alternatives concern how they prevent, defend and control investment disputes and preserve regulatory capacity. For investors, the EU proposal preserves international claims but changes the adjudicative institution; Brazil’s model emphasizes facilitation and prevention and uses state-to-state rather than investor-state dispute settlement. For arbitrators, counsel and arbitral institutions, sustaining reforms retain a central role for existing professional structures, whereas permanent adjudication would alter appointments and institutional roles. Bahrain’s representatives particularly emphasize developing states, emerging arbitration hubs and participation by underrepresented arbitrators. Civil society pressure is presented as helping create the EU’s opportunity for reform. These are investment-governance effects and proposed institutional consequences, not claims about AI-driven legal employment or productivity.
